title: The ten bridesmaids (Matthew 25:1–13)
hookLine: five bring spare oil for a groom who comes late; five run out

cards: It's a wedding night in a village. Ten young women wait with their lamps to meet the groom and walk him in to the feast. Five brought a flask of spare oil.
Five didn't. The groom is late. It gets dark, and all ten nod off.
Then, at midnight, a shout: he's coming! Go out and meet him! They jump up and trim their lamps, and the five without spare oil watch their flames sputter.
Give us some of your oil, they say, our lamps are going out. The other five say no. There might not be enough for all of us.

teach.b: Matthew places this story in the last days before Jesus's arrest. It's about waiting for someone who's late, and Christians have long read it as waiting for Christ to come again.
The ending says so: "Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour." But look closer: "While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept." All ten.
The wise ones fell asleep too. So the story isn't about staying on high alert every minute; nobody manages that.
The difference was settled hours earlier, in daylight, when five of them thought: this might take longer than I expect. I'll bring a little extra. And the refusal to share?
But some things can't be borrowed at the last minute, and readiness is one of them. At midnight you can't borrow someone else's years of practice, or their steadiness, or their prayers.
While the five are off buying oil, the groom arrives, the ready ones go in with him, "and the door was shut."

teach.h: YE KNOW NEITHER THE DAY NOR THE HOUR.
teach.b: It's a hard ending, and the story doesn't soften it. The old King James calls them ten virgins; the Greek word means young unmarried women, which is why modern tellings say bridesmaids.
Nobody's sure what their lamps were: small clay oil lamps, or torches wrapped in oily rags that burn out fast. Either way, the light only lasts as long as the oil.

how: Many Christians hear this story in church in the weeks before Advent, when the readings turn to waiting and being ready, and some keep a habit of preparing the evening before for the day ahead.

practice: Think about the first hour of tomorrow, and what tomorrow-you will wish you'd done tonight: the water bottle filled, the clothes laid out, the line for a hard conversation written down, the thing that always dies charged.
Pick one small thing and picture yourself doing it calmly, without fuss; that's the spare flask. Then let it go, and rest here, the way all ten rested.
